metadata.title: Complex Cobordism vs Representing Formal Group Laws

extraction_notes.note: Borel-Serre's result is stated in full but inside the same sentence as the paper's conclusion that L_{2k}->MU(k) is an equivalence modulo torsion; a sentence cannot be split, so it is one paper claim with Borel-Serre as an assumption.
The Cartan-Leray spectral sequence statement shares its sentence with a remark on the cofiber killing the H_*(k!) summand; kept as one external theorem node.
Uncited standard facts (complex orientation gives an FGL; MU(k) as cofiber, which the paper calls 'surely well-known') marked external standard (uncited); could be read as paper content.

Proofs are informal prose; PP3 includes the strategy paragraphs before the 'We therefore claim' lemma. In Section 6 the argued result (square is a pullback) is announced before its argument, and the final R_k ~ W^k CP is kept in the proof.
Much content is commutative diagrams (xymatrix) and figure captions; the two figure captions are taken as examples of blooms, the diagram-only summary as a remark.

The negative observation that S^{2k-1}*F_k is not highly connected is a claim; its justifying sentence (induction on flag manifolds, pi_1 F_k = k!) is a one-sentence proof node, although it also states new facts.

Sentences end in displayed diagrams with no closing punctuation, and the figure examples exist only as captions; these spans end at the display or caption end, which the checker flags as mid-sentence.
Historical/expository remarks (Betley quotation, Steiner isoperimetric parallel, motivation sentences, the prose restatement of Lemma 1 and the sentence previewing Lemma 2) were not made nodes.

metadata.extraction_comment: The paper is an informal research note: most proofs are heuristic sketches in prose, and the main theorem is introduced by 'We therefore claim'.

nodes.name: Ravenel's question on complex cobordism
nodes.statement:
We attempt to answer a question of D. C. Ravenel's:
``\textit{Infinite loopspace theorists, where are you?}'', or more prosaically:
 Can one start from the notion of Ring Spectrum Representing [Formal Group Laws] (the functor) and arrive at Complex Cobordism?
nodes.statement_short: Can one start from the ring spectrum representing formal group laws and arrive at complex cobordism?

nodes.name: Milnor's theorem; Landweber-Novikov theorem
nodes.statement: Milnor showed that the cohomology ring $MU$ was {\em naturally} isomorphic to Lazard's ring $\Lambda$, while Landweber \cite{landweber} and Novikov \cite{novikov} show the stronger result that the Hopf algebra $(MU^*MU,MU^*)$ {\em naturally} represents Lazard's Hopf algebra.
conclusions: the cohomology ring $MU$ was {\em naturally} isomorphic to Lazard's ring $\Lambda$
the Hopf algebra $(MU^*MU,MU^*)$ {\em naturally} represents Lazard's Hopf algebra
nodes.statement_short: $MU^*$ is naturally Lazard's ring, and $(MU^*MU,MU^*)$ represents Lazard's Hopf algebra.

nodes.name: Notation for complex projective space and its powers
nodes.statement: We write $\mathbb{CP}$ for infinite complex projective space, $\mathbb{CP}_k$ for its usual $2k$-skeleta, and will otherwise (try to) emphasize monoidal structures in superscripts: $\mathbb{CP}^{\times k}$ is a $k$-fold direct product, $\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}$ a $k$-fold smash, et.c.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathbb{CP}$ is infinite complex projective space, $\mathbb{CP}_k$ its skeleta; superscripts denote $k$-fold products or smashes.

nodes.name: Symmetric group $k!$ and Borel quotient notation
nodes.statement:
We use $k!$ as the name of the symmetric group on $[k]$ (the von Neumann ordinal, for definiteness), whose cardinality is the usual significance of ``$k!$'';
Borel quotient is denoted $/\!/ $ and cofiber is $/$; in particular $*/\!/ G \simeq \mathbf{B} G$.
nodes.statement_short: $k!$ denotes the symmetric group on $[k]$; $/\!/$ is Borel quotient and $/$ is cofiber.

nodes.name: Generalized Thom space (twisted half-smash)
nodes.statement:
In any case, our twisted half smashes, or generalized Thom spaces, are denoted and defined as
$$ \rlap{\rule{1pt}{0pt}\rule[.6ex]{.6em}{.4pt}}\mathrm{Th}(X,F) \simeq E/X $$ 
where $X \to E \to X$ is a section/retract with fibers $F\to E \to X$.
nodes.statement_short: The generalized Thom space of a retractive space $E$ over $X$ with fiber $F$ is the cofiber $E/X$.

nodes.name: Thom space of a group action as cofiber of Borel quotients
nodes.statement:
In particular, the Thom space of a group action in the pointed category is a cofiber of Borel quotients:
$$ \rlap{\rule{1pt}{0pt}\rule[.6ex]{.6em}{.4pt}}\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B} G, X) \simeq (X/\!/ G) / (*/\!/ G)  .$$
conclusions: the Thom space of a group action in the pointed category is a cofiber of Borel quotients
nodes.statement_short: $\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B}G,X)\simeq (X/\!/G)/(*/\!/G)$.

nodes.name: Coherent cube
nodes.statement:
In fact what diagrams we use are, almost exclusively, coherent cubes, which are diagrams all of whose cubical facets are ``contractible'', to the extent that makes sense;
 and whenever we say ``colimit'' or ``cofiber'' or ``fiber'' we mean, exclusively, {\em homotopy}-colimit, {\em homotopy}-(co)fiber, et.c.
differentia: all of whose cubical facets are ``contractible''

nodes.name: Distributivity (Mather's cube theorems)
nodes.statement:
Lastly, within the usual Kelley category of CG[w]Hf spaces, one has Mather's Cube theorems; we call the {\em result} of Mather's theorems
 (and its finitary corollaries over any colimit) {\em distributivity}, after the obvious arithmetic analogue.
nodes.statement_short: 'Distributivity' names the conclusion of Mather's cube theorems and their finitary corollaries over colimits.

nodes.name: Finitary distributivity as an axiom of unstable homotopy
nodes.statement:
Note that its use in homotopy is decades older than Mather's published proofs, underlying at least one classic construction of the Leray-Serre spectral sequence,
 (see also in particular the works of Tudor Ganea),
 and we use finitary distributivity as a general {\em axiom} of [unstable] homotopy.

nodes.name: Complex orientation gives a formal group law
nodes.statement:
That is, given a ring spectrum $\Lambda$ (suitable for Atiyah-Hirzebruch purposes) and a class 
 $g : \Lambda^2(\mathbb{CP})$ extending the fundamental class $\eta: \Lambda^2(\mathbb{S}^2)\sim \Lambda^0(*)\ni 1$,
 pull-back along tensor product of lines $\otimes: \mathbb{CP}\times\mathbb{CP} \to \mathbb{CP}$ induces a ring homomorphism
 $\Lambda^*(\mathbb{CP}) \to \Lambda^*(\mathbb{CP}\times\mathbb{CP})$ which (due to the goodness of $g$ and collapsing spectral sequences) gives a formal group law
$$ \Lambda^*(\mathbb{S})[x] \to \Lambda^*(\mathbb{S})[x\otimes 1,1\otimes x] .$$
assumptions: given a ring spectrum $\Lambda$ (suitable for Atiyah-Hirzebruch purposes) and a class $g : \Lambda^2(\mathbb{CP})$ extending the fundamental class $\eta: \Lambda^2(\mathbb{S}^2)\sim \Lambda^0(*)\ni 1$
conclusions: pull-back along tensor product of lines $\otimes: \mathbb{CP}\times\mathbb{CP} \to \mathbb{CP}$ induces a ring homomorphism $\Lambda^*(\mathbb{CP}) \to \Lambda^*(\mathbb{CP}\times\mathbb{CP})$ which (due to the goodness of $g$ and collapsing spectral sequences) gives a formal group law
nodes.statement_short: A complex orientation $g$ of a ring spectrum yields a formal group law via pull-back along tensor product of lines.

nodes.name: Principal tools behind the formal group law
nodes.statement_short: The FGL construction rests on collapse of the Atiyah-Hirzebruch spectral sequence and $H^*(\mathbb{CP})=\mathbb{Z}[x]$, which matches $H_*(\Omega S^{2n+1})$.

nodes.name: Minimal complex-oriented ring spectrum
nodes.statement:
{\em Having} chosen to reflect FGLs by complex-oriented ring spectra, one can clearly ask:
 what is the minimal complex-oriented ring spectrum?  
And this in turn means: what is the ring spectrum $\Lambda$ {\em generated by} a map $\mathbb{CP} \to \Lambda_2$?
nodes.statement_short: Find the ring spectrum freely generated by a map $\mathbb{CP}\to\Lambda_2$.

nodes.name: Model of ring spectra: $E_\infty$ algebras
Spaces $L_{2k}$
nodes.statement:
Using this model (cf. \cite{mayRings}) it is straightforward that our ring spectrum $\Lambda$ should be approximated by the spaces
$$ L_{2k} = \rlap{\rule{1pt}{0pt}\rule[.6ex]{.6em}{.4pt}}\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B} k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}) $$
with prespectrum maps induced by
$$ \mathbb{S}^2 \wedge L_{2k} \to \mathbb{CP} \wedge L_{2k} \to L_{2k+2} $$
nodes.statement_short: $\Lambda$ is approximated by $L_{2k}=\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B}k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k})$ with prespectrum maps through $\mathbb{CP}\wedge L_{2k}$.

nodes.name: Universality of the $L_{2k}$
nodes.statement: But the reason is simple: the $L_{2k}$ are already universal.
conclusions: the $L_{2k}$ are already universal

nodes.name: Proof of universality of $L_{2k}$
nodes.statement_short: Ring maps to any oriented $E$ must make the Thom-space square commute, and this determines the map uniquely from $L_{2k}$.

nodes.name: Direct-sum map $\bigoplus$
nodes.statement:
Since direct sum is plainly a useful $E_\infty$ construction on complex vector spaces (this is, after Segal, what makes $\mathbf{B} U$ an infinite loopspace), it is the most natural thing in geometry to consider the maps
$$ \bigoplus : \mathbb{CP}^{\times k} /\!/  k! \to \mathbf{B} U(k).$$
nodes.statement_short: The direct-sum map $\mathbb{CP}^{\times k}/\!/k!\to\mathbf{B}U(k)$.

nodes.name: Proof that $MU(k)$ is the cofiber of $\mathbf{B}U(k-1)\to\mathbf{B}U(k)$
nodes.statement:
That is: the Thom space is described as the quotient (cofiber) of a (vector space or disk) bundle by the inclusion of the bundle of spheres (at-infinity or unit spheres); but for homotopy purposes, the important feature is the bundle of spheres itself, which is to say the map
$$ E \to \mathbf{B} U(k) $$ whose fibers are the unit spheres of the tautological bundle.  
The usual discussion of disk bundle and sphere-at-infinity acheives the necessary trivial-fibration$\circ$cofibration replacement in any of the classic model-category structures; however, the result of the construction is the (we now don't need to {\em say} ``homotopy'') cofiber.  Therefore, for the purposes of homotopy, it is sufficient to identify the type of the map $E\to U(k)$; but this is easy: the unit sphere is the (Borel, or ordinary) quotient $U(k)/\!/ U(k-1)$; the canonical action of $U(k)$ on this has Borel quotient equivalent to $\mathbf{B} U(k-1)$ and by functoriality of $\mathbf{B}$ the quotient {\em map} is the fiber map
$$ \mathbb{S}^{2k-1} \to \mathbf{B} U(k-1) \to \mathbf{B} U(k) $$
Hence
nodes.statement_short: Reduce the Thom space to the cofiber of the unit sphere bundle, then identify that bundle with $\mathbf{B}U(k-1)\to\mathbf{B}U(k)$ via the fiber sequence of $U(k)/\!/U(k-1)$.

nodes.name: $MU(k)$ as cofiber of classifying spaces
nodes.statement: $$ MU(k) \simeq \mathbf{B} U(k) / \mathbf{B} U(k-1) $$
conclusions: $$ MU(k) \simeq \mathbf{B} U(k) / \mathbf{B} U(k-1) $$

nodes.name: Pasting diagram of pushouts for $\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B}k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k})$
nodes.statement:
There is a pasting diagram of pushouts
$$\begin{xy}\xymatrix{ W^k \mathbb{CP} /\!/ k! \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathbb{CP}^{\times k}/\!/ k! \ar[d] \\
\mathbf{B} k! \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}/\!/ k! \ar[d] \\
{*} \ar[r] & \rlap{\rule{1pt}{0pt}\rule[.6ex]{.6em}{.4pt}}\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B} k!, \mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}) }
\end{xy} $$
conclusions:
There is a pasting diagram of pushouts
$$\begin{xy}\xymatrix{ W^k \mathbb{CP} /\!/ k! \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathbb{CP}^{\times k}/\!/ k! \ar[d] \\
\mathbf{B} k! \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}/\!/ k! \ar[d] \\
{*} \ar[r] & \rlap{\rule{1pt}{0pt}\rule[.6ex]{.6em}{.4pt}}\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B} k!, \mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}) }
\end{xy} $$
nodes.statement_short: $\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B}k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k})$ is the cofiber of $W^k\mathbb{CP}/\!/k!\to\mathbb{CP}^{\times k}/\!/k!$ via pasted pushouts.

nodes.name: Fat wedge $W^k\mathbb{CP}$
nodes.statement: Specifically, $W^k \mathbb{CP}$ is the so-called ``fat wedge'', which we shall study more closely in the next sections.

nodes.name: Comparison diagram of cofiber sequences
nodes.statement_short: The cofiber sequences for $\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B}k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k})$ and $MU(k)$ sit side by side, linked by the direct-sum map.

nodes.name: Cube of coordinate planes
nodes.statement:
In any category with products, for any pointed object $* \to X$ and any $k:\mathbb{N}$ there is a commuting $k$-cube of coordinate planes: the cube of pullbacks of $k$ inclusions
$$ X^{k-1} \to X^k $$ 
which themselves are the fibers {\em at} $*\to X$ of the $k$ defining structure maps $X^k \to X$.
differentia: the cube of pullbacks of $k$ inclusions $$ X^{k-1} \to X^k $$ which themselves are the fibers {\em at} $*\to X$ of the $k$ defining structure maps $X^k \to X$
nodes.statement_short: For pointed $X$, the $k$-cube of pullbacks of the inclusions $X^{k-1}\to X^k$.

nodes.name: Small coordinate-plane cubes ($k=1,2,3$)
nodes.statement:
Small instances of the coordinate planes cube are
$$ * \to X \qquad (k=1) $$
$$ \begin{xy}\xymatrix{ {*} \ar[r] \ar[d] & X \ar[d]^{(*,id)} \\
X \ar[r]_{(id,*)} & X^2 } \end{xy} (k=2) $$
$$ \begin{xy}\xymatrix@=1.2em{
 {*} \ar[rr] \ar[dr] \ar[dd] &  & X \ar[dr] \ar[dd]|\hole\\
    & X \ar[dd] \ar[rr] &  & X^2 \ar[dd] \\
 X \ar[rr]|\hole \ar[dr]   &  & X^2 \ar[dr]  \\ 
  & X^2 \ar[rr] &  & X^3 }\end{xy} (k=3) $$

nodes.name: Blooms and fat wedges $W^k X$
nodes.statement: Though it is more generality than we need, different truncations of these diagrams (\dots the truncations should have a snappy name; I will call them ``blooms'') have colimits that generalize wedge sums, including, in particular, the ``fat wedge''; for the sake of convenience in notating $W^k X /\!/ k!$, we have chosen to index the fat wedges by the dimension of ambient cube defining them, rather than the degree of their petals.
nodes.statement_short: Truncations ('blooms') of the coordinate-plane cube have colimits generalizing wedges, e.g. the fat wedge $W^kX$, indexed by cube dimension.

nodes.name: Wedge of three copies as a bloom
nodes.statement: Example: Wedge of three $X$s; the bloom looks like a sparse parsley inflorescence

nodes.name: Fat wedge $W^3X$ as a bloom
nodes.statement: Example: $W^3 X$; this bloom looks more like a tulip; in both examples, the dotted portions are generated as an initial Kan extension, to the cube, of the (solid-arrow) bloom

nodes.name: Construction of the lifting square
nodes.statement:
Our purpose in reminding the reader of this construction (who likely enough knows it already) is to prepare for the construction of the actual lifting, a map $W^k \mathbb{CP}/\!/ k! \to \mathbf{B} U(k-1)$; since $W^k\mathbb{CP}$ is a {\em colimit}, constructing a map out of it is accomplished by constructing a coherent cube, such as
$$ \begin{xy}\xymatrix@=1.2em{
 {*} \ar[rr] \ar[dr] \ar[dd] &  & \mathbb{CP} \ar[dr] \ar[dd]|\hole\\
    & \mathbb{CP} \ar[dd] \ar[rr] &  & \mathbb{CP}^{\times 2} \ar[dd] \\
 \mathbb{CP} \ar[rr]|\hole \ar[dr]   &  & \mathbb{CP}^{\times 2} \ar[dr]  & & \mbox{(Do I exist?)} \\ 
  & \mathbb{CP}^{\times 2} \ar[rr] &  & \mathbf{B} U(2) }\end{xy} $$
Now, this in itself is {\em not sufficient} for that we want a map on the Borel quotient $W^k\mathbb{CP}/\!/ k!$, of which $W^k\mathbb{CP}$ is just one fiber over $* \to \mathbf{B} k!$; and so we shall also have to take care that our constructed cube is suitably equivariant.

There isn't much choice about the maps towards the terminal vertex in the wanted diagram: we have direct sum, $\mathbb{CP}^{k-1}\to \mathbf{B} U(k-1)$, and anything hugely different is likely to be too forgetful.  We have already described the map $\mathbf{B} U(k-1)\to \mathbf{B} U(k)$ as the tautological sphere bundle over $\mathbf{B} U(k)$
$$ \mathbb{S}^{2k-1} \to \mathbf{B} U(k-1) \to \mathbf{B} U(k) $$
which is to say that a point of $\mathbf{B} U(k-1)$ over $V:\mathbf{B} U(k)$ corresponds to {\em a unit vector in $V$}, which also articulates the sense in which the map $\mathbf{B} U(k-1)\to \mathbf{B} U(k)$ is direct sum {\em with $\mathbb{C}$} and not just {\em any line}; in terms of the space $\mathbf{B} U(k-1)$ as classifier of $k-1$-dimensional complex vector spaces, a unit vector in $V$ corresponds to {\em the orthogonal complement} of that vector; and so a composite $\mathbf{B} U(k-2) \to \mathbf{B} U(k)$ further corresponds to {\em an ordered pair} of orthogonal unit vectors in $V$, and classifies the orthogonal complement of their span, et.c.  What matters for us is: the action of $k!$ on the relevant cubes {\em permutes these orders}; or, for now passing over the action of $k!$, the possible obstruction to homotopy commutativity in 
$$\begin{xy}\xymatrix{ \mathbb{CP}^{\times k-2} \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathbb{CP}^{\times k-1} \ar[d] \\
\mathbb{CP}^{\times k-1} \ar[r] & \mathbf{B} U(k-1) 
}\end{xy}$$
is that the two routes have chosen orthogonal vectors in $V$, the unambiguous vector space specified by the unambiguous composite $\mathbb{CP}^{\times k-2} \to \mathbb{CP}^{\times k} \to \mathbf{B} U(k)$.  To specify the commutativity of the square, it is sufficient to specify a homotopy in unit vectors between these orthogonal two.  Happily, a basis for a complex space induces an inclusion of a real space with a basis, and in a real space with a basis, the positive orthant of the unit sphere does everything we need!  Being described in such dimension-agnostic terms, it is also clear how to generalize the argument to other layers of the cube, and commutativity with the already-known maps to $\mathbf{B} U(k)$.  And, hopefully, the equivariance of the construction is also sufficiently evident.
nodes.statement_short: Build an equivariant coherent cube out of the fat wedge to $\mathbf{B}U(k)$ by direct sums. Each square is filled by a homotopy between orthogonal unit vectors through the positive orthant.

nodes.name: Lifting square and map $\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B}k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k})\to MU(k)$
nodes.statement:
We therefore claim a commutative square
$$ \xymatrix{W^k\mathbb{CP} /\!/ k! \ar[r]\ar[d] & \mathbf{B} U(k-1)\ar[d] \\
\mathbb{CP}^{\times k} /\!/ k! \ar[r] & \mathbf{B} U(k)} $$ and hence a map 
$$ \rlap{\rule{1pt}{0pt}\rule[.6ex]{.6em}{.4pt}}\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B} k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}) \to MU(k) .$$
conclusions:
a commutative square $$ \xymatrix{W^k\mathbb{CP} /\!/ k! \ar[r]\ar[d] & \mathbf{B} U(k-1)\ar[d] \\
\mathbb{CP}^{\times k} /\!/ k! \ar[r] & \mathbf{B} U(k)} $$

a map 
$$ \rlap{\rule{1pt}{0pt}\rule[.6ex]{.6em}{.4pt}}\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B} k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}) \to MU(k) .$$
nodes.statement_short: The fat-wedge inclusion lifts to $\mathbf{B}U(k-1)\to\mathbf{B}U(k)$, inducing a map $\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B}k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k})\to MU(k)$.
nodes.label: liftingsquare

nodes.name: Fiber of the fat wedge inclusion
nodes.statement:
The fiber of including a fat wedge in a product $W^k X \to X^k$, (and therefore the fiber of the map $W^k \mathbb{CP} /\!/ k! \to \mathbb{CP}^{\times k} /\!/ k!$ as well) is, by Distributivity, the $k$-fold self-join of the loopspace $(\Omega X)^{\star k}$; and so we have the small surprise: a fiber sequence
$$ \mathbb{S}^{2k-1} \to W^k\mathbb{CP} /\!/ k! \to \mathbb{CP}^{\times k} /\!/ k! $$
conclusions: the $k$-fold self-join of the loopspace $(\Omega X)^{\star k}$

a fiber sequence
$$ \mathbb{S}^{2k-1} \to W^k\mathbb{CP} /\!/ k! \to \mathbb{CP}^{\times k} /\!/ k! $$
nodes.statement_short: The fiber of $W^kX\to X^k$ is $(\Omega X)^{\star k}$, giving a fiber sequence $S^{2k-1}\to W^k\mathbb{CP}/\!/k!\to\mathbb{CP}^{\times k}/\!/k!$.

nodes.name: The lifting square is a pullback
nodes.statement: In fact, we will argue that the square we already constructed by an interpolation argument (resulting in Lemma \ref{liftingsquare}), is a pullback.
conclusions: is a pullback

nodes.name: Proof that the lifting square is a pullback
nodes.statement_short: Name the pullback $R_k$; fiberwise it is a join of circles, i.e. a bloom colimit, and integrating over $\mathbb{CP}^{\times k}$ identifies $R_k\simeq W^k\mathbb{CP}$.

nodes.name: Cofiber $Y_k$
nodes.statement:
The cofiber --- let us call it $Y_k$ --- is, of course, the Total Cofiber of a pullback square, which means it is also the cofiber of the comparison map between the base $\mathbf{B} U(k)$ and the pushout of the pullback structure maps:
$$\begin{xy}\xymatrix{
W^k\mathbb{CP} /\!/ k! \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathbf{B} U(k-1) \ar[d] \ar@/^/[ddr] \\
\mathbb{CP}^{\times k} /\!/ k! \ar[r] \ar@/_/[drr] & P_k \ar[dr] \\
& & \mathbf{B} U(k) }\end{xy} $$
$$ Y_k \simeq \mathbf{B} U(k) / P_k \simeq MU(k) / \rlap{\rule{1pt}{0pt}\rule[.6ex]{.6em}{.4pt}}\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B} k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k} ) $$
nodes.statement_short: $Y_k$ is the cofiber of $\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B}k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k})\to MU(k)$, equivalently $\mathbf{B}U(k)/P_k$ for the pushout $P_k$.

nodes.name: Fibers of the map presenting $Y_k$
conclusions: the {\em fibers} of the new map presenting $Y_k$ are the join of the vertical and horizontal fibers
nodes.statement_short: The fibers of $P_k\to\mathbf{B}U(k)$ are $S^{2k-1}\star F_k$.

nodes.name: Group $G$ (torus normalizer extension)
nodes.statement:
As plainly as possible, there are a split extension of groups
$$ 1\to \mathbb{T}^k \to G \to k!\to 1 $$ 
and various (conjugate) inclusions
$$ \mathbb{T}^k \to G \to U(k) $$ 
realizing a maximal torus in $U(k)$.  Concretely, one may take $G$ generated by the diagonal matrices and the permutation matrices.
nodes.statement_short: $G$ is the split extension of $k!$ by $\mathbb{T}^k$, generated by diagonal and permutation matrices in $U(k)$.

nodes.name: $\mathbb{CP}^{\times k}/\!/k!\simeq\mathbf{B}G$ and $F_k\simeq U(k)/\!/G$
nodes.statement:
Continuing,
$$ \mathbb{CP}^{\times k}/\!/ k! \simeq \mathbf{B} G $$
$$ F_k \simeq U(k) /\!/ G \simeq (U(k) /\!/ \mathbb{T}^k)/\!/ k! $$
conclusions: $$ \mathbb{CP}^{\times k}/\!/ k! \simeq \mathbf{B} G $$
$$ F_k \simeq U(k) /\!/ G \simeq (U(k) /\!/ \mathbb{T}^k)/\!/ k! $$

nodes.name: $\mathbb{S}^{2k-1}\star F_k$ is not highly connected
nodes.statement: When I began working towards this note, I wanted to tell you how very-connected $\mathbb{S}^{2k-1}\star F_k$ must be, but, alas, it is not!
conclusions: alas, it is not!

nodes.name: Flag manifolds are simply connected; $\pi_1F_k\simeq k!$
nodes.statement:
There is a simple induction argument that each (complex) flag manifold $V_k = U(k)/\!/ \mathbb{T}^k$ is simply connected: there are fiber sequences
$$ V_k \to V_{k+1} \to \mathbb{CP}_k $$
and the base case $V_2 \simeq \mathbb{CP}_1$; this means that $\pi_1 F_k \simeq k!$, so that $\pi_2 \Sigma F_k \simeq C_2 = \mathrm{ab}(k!) $.
nodes.statement_short: By induction via fiber sequences $V_k\to V_{k+1}\to\mathbb{CP}_k$, flag manifolds are simply connected, so $\pi_1F_k\simeq k!$ and $\pi_2\Sigma F_k\simeq C_2$.

nodes.name: Rational cohomology of $L_{2k}$
nodes.statement:
In particular, 
$$ H^*(L_{2k}; \mathbb{Q}) \simeq (H^*(\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k};\mathbb{Q}))^{k!} $$
That is, the rational cohomology of $L_{2k}$ is the $k!$-invariants of the [already-torsion-free] homology of $\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}$ (because for finite $G$, all extensions of finitely-generated $\mathbb{Q}[G]$-modules are split).
conclusions: $$ H^*(L_{2k}; \mathbb{Q}) \simeq (H^*(\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k};\mathbb{Q}))^{k!} $$
nodes.statement_short: Rational cohomology of $L_{2k}$ is the $k!$-invariants of that of $\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}$.

nodes.name: $L_{2k}\to MU(k)$ is an equivalence modulo torsion
nodes.statement:
A result that should be well-known due to Borel+Serre \cite{borSer} that in ordinary cohomology, $H^*(\mathbf{B} U(k),\mathbb{Z}) \to H^*(\mathbb{CP}^{\times k};\mathbb{Z})$ is {\em exactly} the inclusion of the $k!$-invariants; it will follow from this, since we have an explicit-enough factorization of the maps
$$ \mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k} \to \rlap{\rule{1pt}{0pt}\rule[.6ex]{.6em}{.4pt}}\mathrm{Th}(\mathbf{B} k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}) \to MU(k), $$
and from the multiplicative underpinning of the Thom isomorphism, that our map $L_{2k} \to MU(k)$ is an equivalence {\em modulo torsion}.
assumptions: in ordinary cohomology, $H^*(\mathbf{B} U(k),\mathbb{Z}) \to H^*(\mathbb{CP}^{\times k};\mathbb{Z})$ is {\em exactly} the inclusion of the $k!$-invariants
conclusions: our map $L_{2k} \to MU(k)$ is an equivalence {\em modulo torsion}
nodes.statement_short: Via Borel-Serre's identification of $H^*(\mathbf{B}U(k))$ with symmetric invariants and the Thom isomorphism, $L_{2k}\to MU(k)$ is a rational equivalence.

nodes.name: Complex cobordism is the initial torsion-free complex-orientable ring spectrum
nodes.statement: We can therefore, perhaps, give Ravenel the more concrete answer: Complex Cobordism is the initial {\em torsion-free} complex-orientable ring spectrum.
conclusions: Complex Cobordism is the initial {\em torsion-free} complex-orientable ring spectrum

nodes.name: Cartan-Leray spectral sequence
nodes.statement:
The Cartan-Leray spectral sequence tells us
$$ H_p( k! ; H_q(\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k},\mathbb{F})) \Rightarrow H_{p+q} (\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}/\!/  k!) $$ 
while the cofiber map trivializes a direct summand $H_*(k!)\hookrightarrow H_*(\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}/\!/ k!)$, the image of the retract $\mathbf{B} k!$ of $\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}/\!/ k!$.
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
conclusions: $$ H_p( k! ; H_q(\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k},\mathbb{F})) \Rightarrow H_{p+q} (\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}/\!/  k!) $$
nodes.statement_short: Cartan-Leray spectral sequence computing $H_*(\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}/\!/k!)$ from group homology of $k!$; the cofiber kills the $H_*(k!)$ summand.

nodes.name: Homology of $\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}$ as representations
nodes.statement:
The $H_*(\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k})$ happen to be sums of (possibly trivial) tensor products of the tautological representation;
 the rational case of this sequence (and sufficient evidence of its collapse) has already been used in \mbox{section \ref{rescue}}.
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum

nodes.name: Betley's stability theorem
nodes.statement: For any functor $T \in Ab^\Gamma$ of finite degree $d$, the natural map $$H_i( (n-1)! ; T ([n-1])) \to H_i( n! ; T([n])) $$ is an isomorphism provided $2i + d < n$.
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
assumptions: For any functor $T \in Ab^\Gamma$ of finite degree $d$
conclusions: the natural map $$H_i( (n-1)! ; T ([n-1])) \to H_i( n! ; T([n])) $$ is an isomorphism
nodes.statement_short: Homology of symmetric groups with twisted coefficients from a finite-degree functor on $\Gamma$ stabilizes for $2i+d<n$.
nodes.label: betstable

nodes.name: Category $\Gamma$ and degree of a functor
nodes.statement:
Here, $\Gamma$ is the category of {\em partial} maps of finite sets; the {\em degree} of such an Abelian functor is defined there in terms of the joint kernels of forgetting: a functor $T$ is of degree at-most $d$ whenever, for all $d$-part partitions $X = \coprod_j X_j$, the natural maps
$$ T(X) \to \bigoplus_i T(\coprod_{j\neq i} X_j) $$ 
are all injective.
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
nodes.definiendum: degree of an Abelian functor on $\Gamma$
nodes.statement_short: $\Gamma$ is partial maps of finite sets; $T$ has degree $\le d$ if the maps to sums over forgetting one part of any $d$-part partition are injective.

nodes.name: Cell-counting argument for the degree bound
nodes.statement:
For stable-homotopy purposes, we are interested in the homology groups $H_{2k+j}(\rlap{\rule{1pt}{0pt}\rule[.6ex]{.6em}{.4pt}}\mathrm{Th}(k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}))$ for $j\lesssim J$; that is, we are concerned only with the $2k+2J$-skeleton of the smash.  Particularly, the $2k+2J$-skeleton of $\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}$ consists of $\binom{J+k}{J}$ cells (apart from the basepoint).  More: in $\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}$, nontrivial cells are products of $k$ nontrivial cells in $\mathbb{CP}$, of even dimensions, at least $2$; if their total dimension is not more than $2k+2J$, then at most $J$ of the factors are of dimension {\em greater} than $2$; that is, if $k > J$, all the cells in the $2k+2J$-skeleton of $\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}$ are contained in an image of $$ \mathbb{CP}^{\wedge l} \wedge \mathbb{S}^2 \wedge \mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k-l-1} \hookrightarrow \mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k} $$
and an easy amplification of this argument to $J+1$ smash factors leads us to the conclusion:
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
nodes.statement_short: Count cells: in low skeleta of $\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}$ at most $J$ factors exceed dimension 2, so all cells come from smashes containing an $S^2$ factor.

nodes.name: Degree bound for $H_{2k+j}(\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k})$
nodes.statement: $H_{2k+j}(\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k})$, for $j < 2J$, extends along $[k] : \Gamma$ as a functor of degree at most $J$.
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
conclusions: extends along $[k] : \Gamma$ as a functor of degree at most $J$

nodes.name: Stabilization of $H_p(k!;H_{2k+j}(\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}))$
nodes.statement: Consequently $H_p(k!;H_{2k+j}(\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}))$ stabilizes for $2 p + J \leq k$.
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
conclusions: $H_p(k!;H_{2k+j}(\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}))$ stabilizes

nodes.name: Proof that the $L_{2k}$ stabilize
nodes.statement:
This establishes that the pages $E^2_{*,*}$ of the Cartan-Leray spectral sequences are stable in the sense necessary for $L_{2k}$ to approximate a finite-type spectrum; concluding that $L_{2k}$ themselves stabilize reduces to arguing that the prespectrum maps $\Sigma^2 L_{2k} \to \mathbb{CP}\wedge L_{2k} \to L_{2(k+1)}$ {\em realize} the morphisms shown in \mbox{Lemma \ref{betstable}} to become isomorphisms; but this already follows from the usual calculation of $H_i(\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k})$. 

We therefore claim:
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
nodes.statement_short: Stability of the Cartan-Leray $E^2$ pages plus realization of Betley's isomorphisms by the prespectrum maps.

nodes.name: $L_*$ presents the initial complex-oriented commutative ring spectrum
nodes.statement: The spaces $L_{2k}$ with the maps $\Sigma^2 L_{2k} \to L_{2(k+1)}$ approximate a finite-type commutative ring spectrum $\Lambda$; this is the initial complex-oriented commutative ring spectrum.
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
assumptions: The spaces $L_{2k}$ with the maps $\Sigma^2 L_{2k} \to L_{2(k+1)}$
conclusions: approximate a finite-type commutative ring spectrum $\Lambda$
this is the initial complex-oriented commutative ring spectrum
nodes.statement_short: The $L_{2k}$ assemble into a finite-type commutative ring spectrum, the initial complex-oriented one.

nodes.name: Reduce to sphere bundle
nodes.statement:
That is: the Thom space is described as the quotient (cofiber) of a (vector space or disk) bundle by the inclusion of the bundle of spheres (at-infinity or unit spheres); but for homotopy purposes, the important feature is the bundle of spheres itself, which is to say the map
$$ E \to \mathbf{B} U(k) $$ whose fibers are the unit spheres of the tautological bundle.
nodes.statement_short: Thom space is determined by the unit sphere bundle map $E\to\mathbf{B}U(k)$.

nodes.name: Model-independence of cofiber
nodes.statement: The usual discussion of disk bundle and sphere-at-infinity acheives the necessary trivial-fibration$\circ$cofibration replacement in any of the classic model-category structures; however, the result of the construction is the (we now don't need to {\em say} ``homotopy'') cofiber.
nodes.statement_short: The disk/sphere construction is just a model of the homotopy cofiber.

nodes.name: Identify the sphere bundle
nodes.statement:
Therefore, for the purposes of homotopy, it is sufficient to identify the type of the map $E\to U(k)$; but this is easy: the unit sphere is the (Borel, or ordinary) quotient $U(k)/\!/ U(k-1)$; the canonical action of $U(k)$ on this has Borel quotient equivalent to $\mathbf{B} U(k-1)$ and by functoriality of $\mathbf{B}$ the quotient {\em map} is the fiber map
$$ \mathbb{S}^{2k-1} \to \mathbf{B} U(k-1) \to \mathbf{B} U(k) $$
Hence
nodes.statement_short: The sphere bundle is $\mathbf{B}U(k-1)\to\mathbf{B}U(k)$ with fiber $S^{2k-1}$.

nodes.name: Maps out of a colimit via coherent cubes
nodes.statement:
Our purpose in reminding the reader of this construction (who likely enough knows it already) is to prepare for the construction of the actual lifting, a map $W^k \mathbb{CP}/\!/ k! \to \mathbf{B} U(k-1)$; since $W^k\mathbb{CP}$ is a {\em colimit}, constructing a map out of it is accomplished by constructing a coherent cube, such as
$$ \begin{xy}\xymatrix@=1.2em{
 {*} \ar[rr] \ar[dr] \ar[dd] &  & \mathbb{CP} \ar[dr] \ar[dd]|\hole\\
    & \mathbb{CP} \ar[dd] \ar[rr] &  & \mathbb{CP}^{\times 2} \ar[dd] \\
 \mathbb{CP} \ar[rr]|\hole \ar[dr]   &  & \mathbb{CP}^{\times 2} \ar[dr]  & & \mbox{(Do I exist?)} \\ 
  & \mathbb{CP}^{\times 2} \ar[rr] &  & \mathbf{B} U(2) }\end{xy} $$
nodes.statement_short: A map out of the colimit $W^k\mathbb{CP}$ is given by a coherent cube to $\mathbf{B}U(k)$.

nodes.name: Equivariance requirement
nodes.statement: Now, this in itself is {\em not sufficient} for that we want a map on the Borel quotient $W^k\mathbb{CP}/\!/ k!$, of which $W^k\mathbb{CP}$ is just one fiber over $* \to \mathbf{B} k!$; and so we shall also have to take care that our constructed cube is suitably equivariant.
nodes.statement_short: The cube must also be $k!$-equivariant to descend to the Borel quotient.

nodes.name: Maps to the terminal vertex
nodes.statement:
There isn't much choice about the maps towards the terminal vertex in the wanted diagram: we have direct sum, $\mathbb{CP}^{k-1}\to \mathbf{B} U(k-1)$, and anything hugely different is likely to be too forgetful.  We have already described the map $\mathbf{B} U(k-1)\to \mathbf{B} U(k)$ as the tautological sphere bundle over $\mathbf{B} U(k)$
$$ \mathbb{S}^{2k-1} \to \mathbf{B} U(k-1) \to \mathbf{B} U(k) $$
which is to say that a point of $\mathbf{B} U(k-1)$ over $V:\mathbf{B} U(k)$ corresponds to {\em a unit vector in $V$}, which also articulates the sense in which the map $\mathbf{B} U(k-1)\to \mathbf{B} U(k)$ is direct sum {\em with $\mathbb{C}$} and not just {\em any line}; in terms of the space $\mathbf{B} U(k-1)$ as classifier of $k-1$-dimensional complex vector spaces, a unit vector in $V$ corresponds to {\em the orthogonal complement} of that vector; and so a composite $\mathbf{B} U(k-2) \to \mathbf{B} U(k)$ further corresponds to {\em an ordered pair} of orthogonal unit vectors in $V$, and classifies the orthogonal complement of their span, et.c.
nodes.statement_short: Use direct sum to $\mathbf{B}U(k-1)$; points over $V$ are unit vectors (orthogonal frames) in $V$.

nodes.name: Identify obstruction to commutativity
nodes.statement:
What matters for us is: the action of $k!$ on the relevant cubes {\em permutes these orders}; or, for now passing over the action of $k!$, the possible obstruction to homotopy commutativity in 
$$\begin{xy}\xymatrix{ \mathbb{CP}^{\times k-2} \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathbb{CP}^{\times k-1} \ar[d] \\
\mathbb{CP}^{\times k-1} \ar[r] & \mathbf{B} U(k-1) 
}\end{xy}$$
is that the two routes have chosen orthogonal vectors in $V$, the unambiguous vector space specified by the unambiguous composite $\mathbb{CP}^{\times k-2} \to \mathbb{CP}^{\times k} \to \mathbf{B} U(k)$.
nodes.statement_short: The two routes around a square choose orthogonal unit vectors in the same $V$.

nodes.name: Homotopy through positive orthant
nodes.statement: To specify the commutativity of the square, it is sufficient to specify a homotopy in unit vectors between these orthogonal two.  Happily, a basis for a complex space induces an inclusion of a real space with a basis, and in a real space with a basis, the positive orthant of the unit sphere does everything we need!
nodes.statement_short: Fill each square by the path between orthogonal unit vectors in the positive orthant.

nodes.name: Generalize to all layers
nodes.statement: Being described in such dimension-agnostic terms, it is also clear how to generalize the argument to other layers of the cube, and commutativity with the already-known maps to $\mathbf{B} U(k)$.  And, hopefully, the equivariance of the construction is also sufficiently evident.
nodes.statement_short: The construction extends to all layers of the cube, equivariantly.

nodes.name: Name the pullback $R_k$
nodes.statement_short: Working on the $k!$-space, define $R_k$ as the pullback of $\mathbf{B}U(k-1)\to\mathbf{B}U(k)$ along $\oplus$.

nodes.name: Fibers are joins of circles, a bloom colimit
nodes.statement_short: The fiber of $R_k$ over $x$ is the unit sphere of $\oplus x$, a join of circles, which is a bloom colimit.

nodes.name: Integrate over the base
nodes.statement_short: Globally, $R_k$ is the bloom colimit in the coordinate-plane cube of $\mathbb{CP}^{\times k}$.

nodes.name: Conclude $R_k\simeq W^k\mathbb{CP}$
nodes.statement:
Consequently,
$$ R_k \simeq W^k \mathbb{CP} .$$
nodes.statement_short: Hence $R_k\simeq W^k\mathbb{CP}$.

nodes.name: Restrict to a skeleton
nodes.statement: For stable-homotopy purposes, we are interested in the homology groups $H_{2k+j}(\rlap{\rule{1pt}{0pt}\rule[.6ex]{.6em}{.4pt}}\mathrm{Th}(k!,\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}))$ for $j\lesssim J$; that is, we are concerned only with the $2k+2J$-skeleton of the smash.
nodes.statement_short: Only the $2k+2J$-skeleton of the smash matters.
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum

nodes.name: Count cells
nodes.statement: Particularly, the $2k+2J$-skeleton of $\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}$ consists of $\binom{J+k}{J}$ cells (apart from the basepoint).
nodes.statement_short: The skeleton has $\binom{J+k}{J}$ cells.
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum

nodes.name: Cells come from smashes with an $S^2$ factor
nodes.statement:
More: in $\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}$, nontrivial cells are products of $k$ nontrivial cells in $\mathbb{CP}$, of even dimensions, at least $2$; if their total dimension is not more than $2k+2J$, then at most $J$ of the factors are of dimension {\em greater} than $2$; that is, if $k > J$, all the cells in the $2k+2J$-skeleton of $\mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k}$ are contained in an image of $$ \mathbb{CP}^{\wedge l} \wedge \mathbb{S}^2 \wedge \mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k-l-1} \hookrightarrow \mathbb{CP}^{\wedge k} $$
and an easy amplification of this argument to $J+1$ smash factors leads us to the conclusion:
nodes.statement_short: At most $J$ factors exceed dimension 2, so cells lie in images of smashes with an $S^2$ factor; this gives degree $\le J$.
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
